sources.title: Context engineering with Dex Horthy (Pragmatic Engineer podcast, transcript)
sources.note: Full auto-caption transcript read end to end, including sponsor reads.

sources.title: Context engineering with Dex Horthy (newsletter page with 12 key observations, timestamps, referenced posts)
sources.note: Gergely's 12-point summary; some numbers appear only here (30-50%, 2-3x, 300-400K).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The less context window you use, the better outcomes you'll get always.
cards.claim: Less context used always gives better results; the early part of the window is the 'smart zone' and beyond it is the 'dumb zone'.
cards.evidence_detail: Credited to Huntley's Ralph work; no numbers beyond heuristics.
cards.landing: Phase routine: one phase per new session; add an explicit token ceiling to the routine

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: 100K for smaller models, 200K for these like really beefy like Codeex and Opus
cards.claim: Numeric training-wheel limits: stop around 100K tokens for smaller models, about 200K for strong ones; he personally goes to 250-400K by feel (newsletter: 300-400K of a 1M window).
cards.evidence_detail: Personal heuristic, explicitly intuition-based; previously 40% of window, then first 100K after 1M windows arrived.
cards.landing: Phase routine / closing message: context-used check; a stop-and-restart threshold

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: let me delete your end file and try again
cards.claim: The tell that a session is in the dumb zone is the model escalating increasingly extreme attempts to make a test pass; at that point write state to a file and restart at 30-50K tokens.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed behaviour at ~200-300K tokens; remedy is a fresh session with the hard task restated.
cards.landing: Phase routine: a 'stuck on a test' rule that forces a fresh session with a handoff file

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: frontier LLMs can follow about 150 to 250 instructions before it starts to drop off
cards.claim: Models follow roughly 150-250 instructions before adherence drops (a 2025 study, older models; newer ones reportedly better), so instruction budget matters as much as information budget.
cards.evidence_detail: Cites a 2025 study; says a later study (via Laurie Voss) shows improvement; he had not read the data himself.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md length/trim decision (instruction count, not just lines)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: too many conflicting instructions
cards.claim: Context has an instruction budget as well as an information budget; conflicting instructions, and a changed-mind conversation, force the model to compute what to ignore and make far-back instructions half-attended.
cards.evidence_detail: Mechanistic explanation, no experiment.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md: audit for conflicting or stale rules; prose docs that drift from CLAUDE.md

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you're not actually getting a like smarter model
cards.claim: A bigger context window does not make a smarter model; intelligence is the ability to attend to the relevant tokens, so 1M windows are mostly longer conversations, not better reasoning.
cards.evidence_detail: Also his March 2026 tweet that a 1M window for Sonnet 4 is unhinged when people struggle past 100K.
cards.landing: Model/window choice for long verifier sessions; do not rely on 1M windows

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: there's four things in your context window that matter.
cards.claim: Four things matter in a context: size, quality of information (errors compound as fact), missing information (filled by guesses), and trajectory of prior agent actions.
cards.evidence_detail: Framework; trajectory example: past turns of 'change, run tests, fix tests' make the next turn repeat it.
cards.landing: Cold-resume trial design: missing-information check; handoff docs must carry verified facts only

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: time to start over
cards.claim: Phrases like 'you're absolutely right' or 'you're right to push back' signal a trajectory-poisoned session (mistake, user yells, more mistakes); start a new session instead of continuing.
cards.evidence_detail: Autoregressive argument; example from his earlier No Vibes Allowed talk.
cards.landing: Phase routine: restart rule when a reviewer or agent is corrected twice; journal the restart

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you would get a 10k token dock out of it
cards.claim: Research step compresses ~100K tokens of code reading into a ~10K markdown doc, which seeds a fresh context for design and planning (frequent intentional compaction).
cards.evidence_detail: Approximate sizes from RPI practice since Aug 2025.
cards.landing: Phase routine: research artifact then fresh session; ties to the plan comment 'Plan @ sha'

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I don't read the research docs.
cards.claim: Match human attention to model weakness: research is hands-off (models are good at it), design/architecture needs a human in the loop, and plans should be vertical slices not horizontal layers.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes his research/design/plan session split; horizontal plans (DB, service, API, UI) untestable until the end.
cards.landing: Phase routine: where the owner reads (design only); plan template requires vertical slices with a check per slice

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I would rather read five separate little mini diffs
cards.claim: Prefer five small manually verifiable diffs to one 2,000-line change, because a failure in a large diff cannot be localised.
cards.evidence_detail: Judgement from building by hand; no data.
cards.landing: Phase sizing / PR size limit in the routine

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the plans that we were building last summer were actually terrible.
cards.claim: Retraction: the original RPI plans (every line as diff blocks) gave no leverage, got skimmed, and doubled review time because plan and PR were both read; plan reading is anti-leverage.
cards.evidence_detail: Self-correction: they recommended reading plans, then stopped doing it themselves.
cards.landing: Ship plan phase routine: avoid code-level plans; keep plan at design/outline level

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a very powerful lever to get agents to work for longer
cards.claim: A plan doc mainly works as an anchor that keeps an agent working until the plan is done; summer-2025 interest in planning was really about longer agent runs.
cards.evidence_detail: Burrito B2B SaaS example: without a plan, a homepage; with a plan, it keeps going.
cards.landing: Plan acts as completion checklist in the draft PR body

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I throw the docs out and the next time I need research I just do it
cards.claim: Retraction: research/plan docs are tactical, per-task artifacts to throw away; regenerate research fresh because tokens are cheap and stale docs mislead. Specs drift from code, so code stays the source of truth.
cards.evidence_detail: Kept docs for 2-3 months then stopped; cites a year-old spec-kit GitHub issue on spec/code drift.
cards.landing: Knowledge-store design (verified diagnoses) and prose-doc drift; argues for expiry or regeneration over evergreen docs

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I have very few opinions on like what sorts of docs
cards.claim: He has found no one who found it worthwhile to maintain parity between documentation/specs and code; evergreen docs have a poor effort-to-value ratio even if AI could update them.
cards.evidence_detail: Based on people he has seen try; not measured.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md and docs/ trim; the knowledge store must justify its upkeep

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: We built a lights off software factory in July of 2025
cards.claim: Lights-off factory (no human code review) built July 2025 was shut down by November 2025; production broke, Opus 4.1 could not find the root cause, and re-onboarding took about 3 weeks.
cards.evidence_detail: Root cause was a primary key routed through the whole codebase needing a different type; days of digging.
cards.landing: Justifies keeping owner view and human reading of designs; warns against fully unattended phases

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: about three to six months of you shipping all the time with nobody reading
cards.claim: After 3-6 months of shipping with nobody reading the code, the codebase is worse and easier to restart than fix; he expects the interval to shrink as models write faster.
cards.evidence_detail: Own experience; newsletter adds that he thinks it would take under four months today.
cards.landing: Owner review cadence for agent-written code; refactor-in-place loops

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: it's still worth not reading the code for most of the time
cards.claim: Retraction: he once judged unread code worth an occasional two-week manual fix, but no longer believes it, because code volume grew 10x-100x and the problem is getting worse.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as a change of mind after the incident.
cards.landing: Supports reading designs and boundary code even when volume rises

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: cost function of bad architecture and bad program design can't be evaluated
cards.claim: Models are trained on SWE-bench-style fix-reproduction, which cannot score maintainability that bites 3-6 months later, so models are not trained to keep codebases healthy; his idea is a benchmark of 20 features in a row with unknown future requirements.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoned from benchmark design; also praises Cognition's Frontier-Code judge layers but calls them insufficient.
cards.landing: Why the harness needs architecture checks (import-linter contracts) beyond tests

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I don't believe like the model writing the code is the same model reading
cards.claim: Agentic code review raises the floor but cannot be trusted to judge code quality: asked 'is this good' a model says great, asked to critique a coworker's PR it finds faults, so models are sycophantic about code they or peers wrote.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal experience of sycophancy asymmetry; no numbers.
cards.landing: Reviewer prompt framing (refute-by-default, 'a coworker wrote this'); fresh-context refuters

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: none of these things have intuition for software architecture
cards.claim: Replacing code review with agentic testing, agentic review and feedback loops (Sentry, support tickets) leaves no one with architectural intuition, so a 3am failure may be unfixable by the agent; PR review becomes the bottleneck pushing teams to this.
cards.evidence_detail: Tweet March 2026: 1-3 year period of 3am breakage as an existential threat; quoted by host.
cards.landing: Keep human-readable designs and ADRs; do not substitute verifiers for owner understanding

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you can make a problem very verifiable, you can kind of like treat it like a black box
cards.claim: Back pressure: if a problem is verifiable (compiler, tests, linters, CI timing), let the model loop against the check; the core Ralph lesson is automating feedback into the model.
cards.evidence_detail: Huntley's example: Sonnet around the clock, $6K over six weeks, a compiled language; his own CI-speed loop (change, push, subagent watches job, decide).
cards.landing: Backpressure scripts per phase (a runnable check the agent loops on) before review

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: run this llinter fix one thing commit and push
cards.claim: Slow loops: a nightly cron in GitHub Actions runs a linter or anti-pattern check, fixes one thing, opens one PR; now four PRs each morning (e.g. React Doctor, optional-prop narrowing); scale scope only as confidence grows; a human reads every PR.
cards.evidence_detail: HumanLayer's own practice; Kyle shipped a skill to build these; two dimensions: more conditions, more items per run.
cards.landing: Scheduled routine (CI cron) for code-quality PRs; a saved reusable loop workflow

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: not use loops to ship the features that users want
cards.claim: Use loops to improve codebase quality, not to ship features, and read all the code; with a 60,000-line Ralph PR nobody can sign off.
cards.evidence_detail: Distinction between loop uses; incremental and contained loops preferred over a redesigned agentic-first factory.
cards.landing: Scope of any scheduled agent: cleanup only, small PRs

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: build one loop at a time and you should keep them small and contained
cards.claim: Add loops one at a time, small and contained; trigger them from non-human events (Sentry alert, support ticket, failing test, cron); everything except 'stop reading the code' is good advice.
cards.evidence_detail: Advice to teams; no data.
cards.landing: Workflow library: one named, saved workflow per trigger

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: an hour spent over here in planning can save you four hours
cards.claim: Seek leverage: an hour of planning/design can save four hours of implementation fixes; three options (lights off, read everything for 30-50% lift, leverage points for 2-3x faster at near hand-written quality).
cards.evidence_detail: Numbers (30-50%, 2-3x, 99% accuracy, 1:4 hour ratio) from what he sees in teams; not a controlled measurement.
cards.landing: Where to spend verifier effort: design and architecture first, implementation review lighter

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: turn that into a one pager and make sure that's correct
cards.claim: Zoom in layer by layer (sentence, one-pager, three-pager, ten-page outline, code), checking each level, to collapse the set of possible end states; do not sweat the docs but review along the way.
cards.evidence_detail: Uncertainty-narrowing analogy; no measurement.
cards.landing: Phase routine: staged elaboration of each phase with an owner check at the one-pager

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: optimizing for utilization and efficiency of one node in your factory
cards.claim: 'Token harder' (maxing subscriptions, utilisation of one node) optimises the wrong thing; 'token smarter' keeps control, taste and architecture judgement while getting AI value, and is harder to pull off.
cards.evidence_detail: Example: a group chat member with six Claude accounts timed to every 5-hour reset; Goldratt's Theory of Constraints framing.
cards.landing: Effort routing: spend tokens where they remove a bottleneck, not to maximise usage

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: your engineering time is always the bottleneck
cards.claim: Start with the smartest model; optimise cost only at scale (e.g. offload simple steps to a model about 1/1,000th Opus's cost) and only after proving value; engineering effort usually costs more than the tokens saved.
cards.evidence_detail: Make it run, make it right, make it fast; 'millions of requests' threshold.
cards.landing: Effort routing: do not hand-tune model tiers per verifier without measured cost; counterweight to cheap-model routing

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: how do I raise the floor so that every single turn
cards.claim: Harness engineering is optimising the integration points of a coding agent (commands, MCPs, skills, codebase organisation); Fowler's inner harness (vendor tools) vs outer harness (what the user customises) is the best definition.
cards.evidence_detail: Definition; credits LangChain and Martin Fowler.
cards.landing: Names FixFlow's .claude/ surface (agents, skills, CLAUDE.md) as the outer harness

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you need to go down a level and think about what's everything
cards.claim: Frameworks get you to 80%; going from 80% to 95-99% requires controlling exactly what goes in the context window and in what order; own the inputs to every LLM step.
cards.evidence_detail: Based on ~100 conversations with AI engineers who discarded frameworks.
cards.landing: Prefer explicit, owned workflow scripts over generic orchestration frameworks

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: how can we add another checkpoint in that factory
cards.claim: Add a human checkpoint before code (design review, planning, shared real-time review) rather than only at the PR; a rework loop after a bad PR is costly and committed direction is hard to steer, so restart rather than loop.
cards.evidence_detail: HumanLayer product thesis ('kill the pull request'); no numbers.
cards.landing: Phase routine: owner checkpoint at design before implementation

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Refactoring, clean code, the pragmatic programmer
cards.claim: Classic software-design books (Refactoring, Clean Code, The Pragmatic Programmer) are more relevant now; his team spends effort on program design (interfaces, seams, dependency injection) so agents can maintain code.
cards.evidence_detail: Closing book recommendation and earlier remarks on program design.
cards.landing: Slice-boundary rules and import-linter contracts as the program-design guard

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we can teach somebody, I think, to be a really good AI developer in a few months
cards.claim: Hiring: strong CS fundamentals are hard to teach in 3 months, while AI-development intuition can be built in a few months.
cards.evidence_detail: Hiring heuristic.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious

gaps: The newsletter page is a summary plus show notes; the 'Transcript' mentioned on it was not in the fetched text, so the YouTube auto-caption transcript was the primary text.
Referenced posts (Skill Issue harness-engineering blog, Fowler article, token harder/smarter thread, kill-the-pull-request post) were seen only as embedded excerpts or mentions, not opened.
Auto-caption errors exist (e.g. 'Ryan Leopo', 'Dystra', 'GPT OSS 12B' for 120B); card quotes are verbatim captions or lightly joined, one quote (R19-33) is a short paraphrased list from the caption.
The 'RPI, what you got wrong' retractions are partial; exact number of RPI stages and the 'design doc' stage are described only briefly.
